title: Towards reliable land cover mapping under domain shift: An overview and comprehensive comparative study on uncertainty estimation
relevance: The review written for our exact situation - land cover mapping where the deployment domain differs from training - comparing uncertainty-estimation methods head to head rather than proposing another. Tells us which uncertainty estimator to use for the per-crown validity intervals and, critically, which ones stay meaningful once the domain shifts, since most are validated in-domain only. This should be read before any further work on calibration or confidence, and before committing to an uncertainty method for the deliverable.

title: Can you trust your model's uncertainty? Evaluating predictive uncertainty under dataset shift
source: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32 (NeurIPS 2019), 13969-13980 (arXiv:1906.02530)
relevance: The canonical result that model confidence degrades as the domain shifts and that post-hoc temperature scaling, fitted on in-distribution validation data, does NOT hold up under shift - accuracy falls and confidence does not fall with it. Directly governs our plan to fix near-threshold misses by calibration: a temperature fitted on 2020 will not transfer to 2000, so calibration must be fitted PER YEAR on in-year data or it inherits the same problem as the labels. Also finds deep ensembles the most robust option under shift, which is a cost we would have to budget for across 18 years.

authors: Ding, Z., Han, X., Liu, P. & Niethammer, M.
title: Local temperature scaling for probability calibration
relevance: Extends temperature scaling from one global scalar to a spatially varying field, so calibration can differ across the image. Matters for us because our miscalibration is spatially structured, not uniform: the model behaves differently on suburban/ornamental ground than on forest stands, which is the 8/8 visual grounding and the ccap_only low-height mass. A single per-year temperature may therefore under-correct exactly where we need it most; this gives the machinery for a context-varying correction.

title: Uncertainty quantification for probabilistic machine learning in earth observation using conformal prediction
relevance: Conformal prediction gives distribution-free coverage guarantees from a modest calibration set - the property our per-crown validity intervals actually need, since we can promise coverage without assuming the model is well specified. Applied to earth observation specifically, so the practicalities (calibration set size, exchangeability assumptions) are worked through for our data type. The exchangeability assumption is where it will bite us: our years are not exchangeable with each other, so conformal must be calibrated within a year, not pooled across the series.
